meta.title: Who really said "The music business is a cruel and shallow money trench, a long plastic hallway where thieves and pimps run free, and good men die like dogs. There's also a negative side"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not about music: Hunter S. Thompson wrote this of the TV business in a 1985 Examiner column. The music version and 'negative side' tag are later alterations.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The music business is a cruel and shallow money trench, a long plastic hallway where thieves and pimps run free, and good men die like dogs. There's also a negative side'?
meta.ogDescription: Hunter S. Thompson wrote this about TV, not music (Examiner, 1985; Generation of Swine, 1988). The 'There's also a negative side' tag isn't his.

answer.label: Not Hunter S. Thompson — a reworded version of his line about TV
answer.sourceLine: Thompson wrote the “money trench” and “long plastic hallway” lines about the TV business, not music, in a San Francisco Examiner column of November 4, 1985, later collected in Generation of Swine (1988). The “music business” wording and the punchline “There’s also a negative side” are later changes that are not in his published text.

source.heading: What Thompson actually wrote

docMeta.dd: Generation of Swine: Tales of Shame and Degradation in the ’80s
New York: Summit Books, 1988 (p. 43, per David Emery)
The TV business (TV journalism), not music

source.excerpt: The TV business is uglier than most things. It is normally perceived as some kind of cruel and shallow money trench through the heart of the journalism industry, a long plastic hallway where thieves and pimps run free and good men die like dogs, for no good reason. Which is more or less true. For the most part, they are dirty little animals with huge brains and no pulse.
trail: A reader sent the urban-legends writer David Emery the exact “music business … There’s also a negative side” wording, and Emery found that and several other versions (TV, radio, corporate communications, show business) all over the web, almost never with a source. Emery, page 1 (archived) ↗

Emery traced it to page 43 of Generation of Swine (Summit Books, 1988): the passage is about the TV business. He dates the column to the San Francisco Examiner of November 4, 1985, and says the “negative side” tag is “nowhere to be found in the original article.” Emery, page 2 (archived) ↗

Wikiquote gives the TV-business passage under Generation of Swine (1988), notes the November 4, 1985 Examiner date, and cites Emery for the finding that Thompson did not write “There’s also a negative side.” Wikiquote: Hunter S. Thompson ↗
In 2007 John Gruber passed on the correction: the popular music-business quote is “a widely-cited misquote,” and the real passage is about the TV industry. Daring Fireball ↗
source.excerptNote: The text as David Emery transcribed it from page 43 of the 1988 Summit Books edition. It has no “music business” and no “There’s also a negative side.”

author.metaLine: 1937–2005 · American journalist, author and founder of Gonzo journalism
author.bio: Hunter S. Thompson was the American writer behind Hell’s Angels and Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas, and the founder of Gonzo journalism. From 1985 he wrote a column for the San Francisco Examiner, and the columns were collected in Generation of Swine (1988). One of those columns attacked the business of TV journalism, and it is the real source of this much-altered quote.

misattribution.heading: How a line about TV became a line about music
misattribution.intro: The passage gets reworded to fit whatever industry the speaker resents, and a joke punchline was added along the way. David Emery found at least half a dozen versions on the web, and almost none of them named a source.

items.why: Thompson wrote “The TV business is uglier than most things,” about TV journalism. Emery stresses that the piece “was not about the music industry.” Emery (archived) ↗
This tag is not in Thompson’s published text. Emery calls it a “nice joke, but Thompson didn’t write it,” and Wikiquote repeats his finding. Wikiquote ↗

Emery recorded versions that put radio, show business and “the corporate communications world” in place of TV. Emery, page 1 (archived) ↗ A radio-engineering blog notes the line is often heard as “The Radio business …” Engineering Radio ↗

items.who: “cruel and shallow money trench, a long plastic hallway”
items.why: The original reads “some kind of cruel and shallow money trench through the heart of the journalism industry” and ends “for no good reason.” The popular version cuts both the journalism framing and that ending. Daring Fireball ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The imagery is Thompson’s, but it describes the TV business, in his San Francisco Examiner column of November 4, 1985, collected in Generation of Swine (1988). “Music business” and “There’s also a negative side” are later changes. Emery’s investigation ↗

context.heading: Why it spread
lead: The line spreads because it fits almost any industry. Emery notes how “sardonically true” it sounds whatever business is named, and that is exactly why people keep swapping in their own. Musicians and music writers made the music version the best known, often with the deadpan “There’s also a negative side” added as a punchline.

Thompson’s actual target was TV journalism. In his San Francisco Examiner column he called it a “cruel and shallow money trench through the heart of the journalism industry.” The Examiner columns were collected in Generation of Swine (Summit Books, 1988).
context.pull: “It was about television. Period.” — David Emery

Emery page 1: a reader asked about the exact wording 'The music business is a cruel and shallow money trench, a long plastic hallway where thieves and pimps run free, and good men die like dogs. There's also a negative side'; Emery lists variants for TV, radio, the corporate communications world and show business; the tag was sometimes included and sometimes not

Emery page 2: the passage is near the bottom of page 43 of Generation of Swine (New York: Summit Books, 1988), begins 'The TV business is uglier than most things', and continues 'Which is more or less true. For the most part, they are dirty little animals with huge brains and no pulse.' It was first published as a bylined San Francisco Examiner column on November 4, 1985; it was not about the music industry ('It was about television. Period.'); the 'negative side' tag is nowhere in the original ('Nice joke, but Thompson didn't write it')
Daring Fireball (17 Sept 2007): the music-business quote is a widely cited misquote; the actual passage is about the TV industry and ends 'for no good reason'
